name: Package apps with Helm
objective: CKAD › Application Deployment. Drill EVERY Helm and Kustomize corner harder than the exam: scaffold+install a release, override values with --set and a values file, inspect release state and revisions, render without installing, apply a Kustomize base, layer transforms (namePrefix + commonLabels + replicas), generate a ConfigMap, and a no-hint diagnose-and-fix. Graded exactly, per requirement.

questions.title: Helm: scaffold a chart and install a release
questions.teach:
**Helm** packages manifests as a **chart** and each deployment as a **release**. `helm create <name>` scaffolds a chart; `helm install <release> <chart> -n <ns>` renders and applies it. The default chart names its Deployment `<release>-<chart>`, so here it is `demo-webapp`.

**Gotcha:** plain `helm install` fails if the release name already exists — `helm upgrade --install` is the idempotent form.
questions.prompt:
Namespace `helm-learn` already exists. Scaffold a chart named `webapp` on the host (e.g. `cd /tmp && helm create webapp`), then install a release named `demo` of it into `helm-learn`.

Target: a release Secret of type `helm.sh/release.v1` for release `demo` exists in `helm-learn`, AND the chart's Deployment `demo-webapp` is present there.
questions.hint: `cd /tmp && helm create webapp`, then `helm install demo /tmp/webapp -n helm-learn`. Check with `helm list -n helm-learn` and `kubectl get deploy demo-webapp -n helm-learn`.
questions.solution:
cd /tmp
helm create webapp
helm install demo /tmp/webapp -n helm-learn
helm list -n helm-learn
kubectl get deploy demo-webapp -n helm-learn

verification.description: helm release 'demo' Secret (helm.sh/release.v1) and Deployment demo-webapp exist in helm-learn

questions.eli5:
Imagine shipping furniture. Instead of mailing a hundred loose screws and planks, you send one neat **flat-pack box** with all the parts and an instruction booklet. **Helm** is that: a **chart** is the flat-pack box of Kubernetes manifests (Deployment, Service, etc.) bundled together.

- `helm create webapp` makes a brand-new flat-pack box called `webapp`, pre-filled with a working example (an nginx Deployment, a Service, and so on).
- `helm install demo /tmp/webapp -n helm-learn` is you actually *assembling* one copy of that furniture in a room. That assembled copy is called a **release**, and you named it `demo`.

Helm remembers every release it assembled by stashing a little record (a **Secret**) in the namespace. The default chart names things `<release>-<chart>`, so your Deployment comes out as `demo-webapp`.

**Watch out:**

- `helm install` **fails if a release with that name already exists** in the namespace ("cannot re-use a name that is still in use"). The safe, repeatable form is `helm upgrade --install demo /tmp/webapp` — it installs if missing, upgrades if present.
- The **release name** (`demo`) and the **chart name** (`webapp`) are different things; the Deployment is `demo-webapp` = release + chart.
- Releases are **namespace-scoped** — install into `-n helm-learn`, and you must use that same `-n` to see it later.
- `helm create` only scaffolds files on your machine; nothing hits the cluster until you `install`.
- Helm's bookkeeping lives in a Secret of type `helm.sh/release.v1` — that's how `helm list` knows the release exists.
questions.deepDive:
## Helm: scaffold a chart and install a release — full rundown

### Mental model
Helm is the Kubernetes package manager. Three nouns:
- **Chart** — a versioned bundle of templated manifests (`Chart.yaml`, `values.yaml`, `templates/`).
- **Release** — one named, installed instance of a chart in a namespace. Install the same chart twice → two releases.
- **Values** — the knobs that parameterize a chart's templates.

Helm stores each release's state server-side in a **Secret** of type `helm.sh/release.v1`, one per revision, in the release's namespace.

### Scaffolding
```bash
cd /tmp
helm create webapp           # creates ./webapp with a working nginx example
```
Chart layout:
```
webapp/
  Chart.yaml        # name, version, appVersion
  values.yaml       # default values (replicaCount, image.repository, image.tag, service...)
  templates/        # deployment.yaml, service.yaml, _helpers.tpl, ...
```

### Installing
```bash
helm install demo /tmp/webapp -n helm-learn
#            ^release ^chart-path  ^namespace
```
The default chart names objects `<release>-<chart>` via the `fullname` helper → Deployment `demo-webapp`.

### install vs upgrade --install
| Command | Behavior |
|---|---|
| `helm install demo ./webapp` | fails if release `demo` already exists |
| `helm upgrade demo ./webapp` | fails if release `demo` does **not** exist |
| `helm upgrade --install demo ./webapp` | **idempotent**: install if absent, upgrade if present |

`upgrade --install` is the standard, repeatable form.

### Verifying
```bash
helm list -n helm-learn                       # NAME demo, REVISION 1, STATUS deployed
helm status demo -n helm-learn
kubectl get deploy demo-webapp -n helm-learn
kubectl get secret -n helm-learn \
  -l owner=helm,name=demo                      # helm.sh/release.v1 secret(s)
```

### Useful install-time flags
| Flag | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `-n, --namespace` | target namespace |
| `--create-namespace` | create ns if missing |
| `--set k=v` | inline value override |
| `-f values.yaml` | values file override |
| `--dry-run` | render + validate, don't install |
| `--wait` | block until resources are Ready |
| `--version` | chart version (for repo charts) |

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **`helm install` is not idempotent** — re-running fails with "cannot re-use a name." Use `upgrade --install`.
- **Release name ≠ chart name**: default object names are `<release>-<chart>` (`demo-webapp`).
- **Namespace-scoped**: Helm's release Secrets live in the namespace; forget `-n` and the release looks missing.
- `helm create` writes **local files only**; nothing is deployed until `install`.
- The chart path can be a directory, a `.tgz`, or `repo/chart` (after `helm repo add`).
- Helm 3 has **no Tiller** — state is Secrets in the namespace, not a cluster-wide component.

### Quick reference
```bash
cd /tmp && helm create webapp
helm install demo /tmp/webapp -n helm-learn        # or: helm upgrade --install
helm list -n helm-learn
kubectl get deploy demo-webapp -n helm-learn
```

questions.title: Helm: override a value on upgrade (--set)
questions.teach:
Charts expose knobs through **values**. Override one without editing chart files via `helm upgrade <release> <chart> --set <key>=<value>` — Helm re-renders and patches the live objects. The default chart's `replicaCount` flows into the Deployment's `spec.replicas`.

**Gotcha:** `helm upgrade` still needs the chart reference (`helm upgrade demo /tmp/webapp ...`), not just the release name.
questions.prompt:
Upgrade the `demo` release so its Deployment runs **4** replicas, by overriding `replicaCount` with `--set` (do not edit the chart files).

Target: Deployment `demo-webapp` in `helm-learn` has `spec.replicas: 4`.
questions.hint: `helm upgrade demo /tmp/webapp -n helm-learn --set replicaCount=4`, then `kubectl get deploy demo-webapp -n helm-learn -o jsonpath='{.spec.replicas}'`.
questions.solution:
helm upgrade demo /tmp/webapp -n helm-learn --set replicaCount=4
kubectl get deploy demo-webapp -n helm-learn -o jsonpath='{.spec.replicas}'   # 4

verification.description: demo-webapp Deployment scaled to 4 replicas via helm --set

questions.eli5:
That flat-pack furniture came with adjustable settings — like a desk whose height you can change without rebuilding it. In Helm those settings are called **values**, and the chart author decides which ones you're allowed to turn.

One of the knobs on the default chart is `replicaCount` — how many copies of the app run. You want 4. Instead of opening the box and editing the instruction booklet, you just **tell Helm the new setting** at upgrade time:

`helm upgrade demo /tmp/webapp -n helm-learn --set replicaCount=4`

Helm re-reads the chart, plugs in your new value, re-renders the manifests, and patches the live Deployment to `replicas: 4`. The chart files on disk stay untouched — you only overrode a value.

**Watch out:**

- **`helm upgrade` still needs the chart reference.** It's `helm upgrade demo /tmp/webapp ...`, not just `helm upgrade demo`. Helm has to re-render from the chart, so you must point at it again.
- `--set` takes **dotted paths** (`image.tag=1.25`) and the key must be a real value the chart uses; a made-up key does nothing visible.
- Every `upgrade` bumps the **revision number** — useful later for `helm history` and `helm rollback`.
- Overriding a value does **not** edit the chart's `values.yaml`; the override lives in the release's stored state, not the files.
- Watch types: `--set replicaCount=4` is fine, but `--set` can misparse commas and dots — wrap tricky values or use a values file (next step).
questions.deepDive:
## Helm: override a value on upgrade (`--set`) — full rundown

### Mental model
Charts are parameterized by **values**. The chart ships defaults in `values.yaml`; you override them at install/upgrade time *without editing chart files*. `--set` supplies an override on the command line; Helm merges it over the defaults, re-renders the templates, and patches the live objects. In the default chart, `replicaCount` maps to the Deployment's `spec.replicas`.

### The command
```bash
helm upgrade demo /tmp/webapp -n helm-learn --set replicaCount=4
#            ^release ^chart ^ns              ^override
kubectl get deploy demo-webapp -n helm-learn -o jsonpath='{.spec.replicas}'   # 4
```

### `--set` syntax
| Form | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `--set replicaCount=4` | scalar |
| `--set image.tag=1.25` | nested key (dot path) |
| `--set a.b.c=v` | deep nesting |
| `--set list[0]=x` | list index |
| `--set a=b,c=d` | multiple (comma-separated) |
| `--set name=null` | explicitly unset |
| `--set-string port=8080` | force string (avoid numeric coercion) |

Escape literal dots/commas with `\`: `--set app\.kubernetes\.io/name=web`.

### Value precedence (lowest → highest)
```
chart values.yaml  <  -f values-file  <  --set  <  --set-string / --set-file
```
`--set` beats `-f`; later `-f` files beat earlier ones.

### Revisions
Every `install`/`upgrade` creates a new **revision** and a new release Secret:
```bash
helm history demo -n helm-learn      # list revisions + status
helm rollback demo 1 -n helm-learn   # revert to revision 1 (creates a NEW revision)
```

### Inspecting what values are in effect
```bash
helm get values demo -n helm-learn            # user-supplied overrides
helm get values demo -n helm-learn -a         # all computed values
helm get manifest demo -n helm-learn          # rendered manifests for the release
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **`helm upgrade` needs the chart reference** (`helm upgrade demo /tmp/webapp`), not just the release name — it re-renders from the chart.
- **`--set` does not edit `values.yaml`** — the override is stored in the release state only.
- **Type coercion**: `--set` may turn `01` or `1.25` into numbers; use `--set-string` when you need a literal string.
- **Comma/dot pitfalls**: unescaped `,`/`.` are parsed as separators; escape them or use `-f`.
- **Each upgrade bumps the revision** — important for `history`/`rollback` questions.
- Overriding a **nonexistent** value silently does nothing visible — confirm the key exists in `values.yaml`.

### Quick reference
```bash
helm upgrade demo /tmp/webapp -n helm-learn --set replicaCount=4
kubectl get deploy demo-webapp -n helm-learn -o jsonpath='{.spec.replicas}'   # 4
helm get values demo -n helm-learn
helm history demo -n helm-learn
```

questions.title: Helm: override the image tag with a values file
questions.teach:
For many or persistent overrides, write a YAML **values file** and pass it with `-f`: `helm upgrade <release> <chart> -f values.override.yaml`. Keys mirror the chart's `values.yaml` structure. The default chart maps `image.tag` into the container image as `<repository>:<tag>`.

**Gotcha:** `-f` and `--set` can combine, and `--set` wins — on a tie the command-line value overrides the file.
questions.prompt:
Still overriding (not editing the chart): set the `demo` release's container image **tag** to `1.25` using a **values file** (`-f`). The default chart's image repository is `nginx`, so the container image becomes `nginx:1.25`.

Target: the first container of Deployment `demo-webapp` in `helm-learn` has image ending in `:1.25` (i.e. `nginx:1.25`). Keep replicas at 4.
questions.hint: Write `/tmp/override.yaml` with `image:\n  tag: "1.25"`, then `helm upgrade demo /tmp/webapp -n helm-learn -f /tmp/override.yaml --set replicaCount=4`. Verify the container image: `kubectl get deploy demo-webapp -n helm-learn -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].image}'`.
questions.solution:
cat > /tmp/override.yaml <<'YAML'
image:
  tag: "1.25"
YAML
helm upgrade demo /tmp/webapp -n helm-learn -f /tmp/override.yaml --set replicaCount=4
kubectl get deploy demo-webapp -n helm-learn -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].image}'   # nginx:1.25

verification.description: demo-webapp container image tag is 1.25 (via -f values file), replicas still 4

questions.eli5:
`--set` is great for one quick knob. But when you have *many* settings, or you want to keep a tidy, reusable record of them, you write them all down in a little note and hand the whole note to Helm. That note is a **values file**.

It's the difference between shouting one instruction to a barista versus handing them a written order with everything on it. You pass the note with `-f`:

```
image:
  tag: "1.25"
```

```
helm upgrade demo /tmp/webapp -n helm-learn -f /tmp/override.yaml --set replicaCount=4
```

The keys in the note **mirror the chart's `values.yaml` structure**. The default chart builds the container image as `<repository>:<tag>`, and the repository is `nginx`, so setting `image.tag: "1.25"` makes the image `nginx:1.25`. Notice you keep `--set replicaCount=4` too, so the replicas you set earlier don't get lost.

**Watch out:**

- **`-f` and `--set` combine, and `--set` wins.** If both set the same key, the command-line `--set` value beats the file.
- The note's **structure must match the chart's `values.yaml`** exactly — `image.tag`, not `imageTag`. Wrong nesting = silently ignored.
- **Quote version tags**: write `tag: "1.25"`, not `tag: 1.25`, or YAML may read it as a number and mangle it.
- Values you don't restate are taken from the chart defaults — that's *why* you re-pass `--set replicaCount=4`, so an earlier override isn't dropped on this upgrade.
- You can pass **multiple `-f` files**; later ones override earlier ones.
questions.deepDive:
## Helm: override with a values file (`-f`) — full rundown

### Mental model
A **values file** is a YAML document whose keys mirror the chart's `values.yaml`. You pass it with `-f`/`--values` so Helm merges it over the chart defaults at render time. Values files are the durable, reviewable way to carry many overrides (vs ad-hoc `--set`). The default chart composes the container image as `<image.repository>:<image.tag>`.

### The override file + command
```yaml
# /tmp/override.yaml
image:
  tag: "1.25"          # quoted → stays a string
```
```bash
helm upgrade demo /tmp/webapp -n helm-learn \
  -f /tmp/override.yaml \
  --set replicaCount=4                    # keep replicas at 4 on this upgrade
kubectl get deploy demo-webapp -n helm-learn \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].image}'   # nginx:1.25
```
With repository `nginx` and tag `1.25`, the rendered image is `nginx:1.25`.

### Value precedence (lowest → highest)
```
chart values.yaml  <  -f file1  <  -f file2 (later wins)  <  --set  <  --set-string/--set-file
```
- Multiple `-f`: **rightmost file wins** on a key tie.
- `--set` always beats any `-f`.

### Keys mirror values.yaml
```bash
helm show values /tmp/webapp        # see the full default values tree
# then mirror the exact nesting in your override file:
#   image:
#     repository: nginx
#     tag: "1.25"
```
Wrong nesting (`imageTag: "1.25"`) is silently ignored — it must match the chart's structure.

### Why re-pass replicaCount
Each `upgrade` re-renders from chart defaults + the overrides you give **this time**. If you drop `--set replicaCount=4`, the Deployment reverts to the chart default (1). Overrides are not "sticky" across upgrades unless re-supplied or baked into a values file.

### Inspecting results
```bash
helm get values demo -n helm-learn            # overrides in effect
helm get manifest demo -n helm-learn          # final rendered YAML
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **`--set` overrides `-f`** on a key tie — remember the precedence order.
- **Unquoted numeric-looking tags** (`tag: 1.25`) may be parsed as a float; **quote** them.
- **Structure must match `values.yaml`** exactly; mismatched keys are ignored, not errored.
- **Overrides aren't sticky** — re-pass or persist them; dropping `--set replicaCount=4` reverts replicas.
- Multiple `-f` files are allowed; **order matters** (last wins).
- `-f` takes a **file path**; `--set` takes inline `k=v`.

### Quick reference
```bash
helm show values /tmp/webapp                  # discover the values tree
cat > /tmp/override.yaml <<'YAML'
image:
  tag: "1.25"
YAML
helm upgrade demo /tmp/webapp -n helm-learn -f /tmp/override.yaml --set replicaCount=4
kubectl get deploy demo-webapp -n helm-learn \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].image}'    # nginx:1.25
```

questions.title: Helm: inspect release state and revision
questions.teach:
`helm list -n <ns>` shows each release with its status and **revision** number; every `install`/`upgrade` bumps the revision. A status of `deployed` (not `failed`/`superseded`) confirms the last operation succeeded. The current revision's state lives in a Secret labelled `status=deployed`.

**Gotcha:** `helm list`/`status` are namespace-scoped — omit `-n <ns>` and a release looks "missing"; use `-A` when unsure.
questions.prompt:
After two upgrades, confirm the `demo` release is **deployed** and now on **revision 3** in `helm-learn`.

Target: the deployed-state release Secret for `demo` carries labels `status=deployed` and `version=3` (`helm list -n helm-learn` shows REVISION 3, STATUS deployed).
questions.hint: `helm list -n helm-learn` → REVISION 3, STATUS deployed. The deployed state Secret is labelled `owner=helm,status=deployed,name=demo,version=3`: `kubectl get secret -n helm-learn -l owner=helm,status=deployed,name=demo --show-labels`.
questions.solution:
helm list -n helm-learn
helm status demo -n helm-learn
kubectl get secret -n helm-learn -l owner=helm,status=deployed,name=demo -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.labels.version}'   # 3

verification.description: release 'demo' is deployed and on revision 3 in helm-learn

questions.eli5:
Every time you assemble or tweak that furniture, Helm keeps a little logbook — like a receipt drawer. Each `install` or `upgrade` adds a new numbered receipt. This step is just *reading the drawer* to confirm where things stand.

Two things to check:

- **Status** — is the last operation healthy? `deployed` means the most recent change went in cleanly. Other words like `failed` or `superseded` tell you something older or broken.
- **Revision** — how many times has this release changed? You started at revision 1 (install), then did two upgrades, so you're now on **revision 3**. Each receipt is numbered.

`helm list -n helm-learn` shows both at a glance — the release name, its STATUS, and its REVISION. Under the hood, Helm's "current" receipt is a Secret labelled `status=deployed` and `version=3`.

**Watch out:**

- **`helm list` and `helm status` are namespace-scoped.** Leave off `-n helm-learn` and the release looks like it vanished. Use `-A` (all namespaces) when you're not sure where it lives.
- **Revision counts every change**, including rollbacks — a rollback doesn't go "back" to an old number, it creates a *new* higher revision.
- Only **one** revision is `deployed` at a time; older ones become `superseded`. Don't panic at `superseded` — it just means "not the current one."
- `helm list` by default hides failed/other-status releases; add `-a` (`--all`) to see everything.
- The revision number and status live in the release **Secret's labels** (`version`, `status`) — handy when a validator checks them directly.
questions.deepDive:
## Helm: inspect release state and revision — full rundown

### Mental model
Helm tracks each release as a series of **revisions**. Every `install`/`upgrade`/`rollback` creates a new revision and a new release **Secret** (`helm.sh/release.v1`) in the namespace. Exactly one revision is the current **`deployed`** state; older ones become **`superseded`**. Reading this state tells you whether the last operation succeeded and which revision is live.

### The commands
```bash
helm list -n helm-learn
# NAME  NAMESPACE   REVISION  STATUS    CHART         APP VERSION
# demo  helm-learn  3         deployed  webapp-0.1.0  1.16.0

helm status demo -n helm-learn        # status + notes of current revision
helm history demo -n helm-learn       # every revision with status
```
Revision math here: `install` = rev 1, first `upgrade` = rev 2, second `upgrade` = rev 3 → **deployed, revision 3**.

### Release statuses
| Status | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `deployed` | current, successful revision |
| `superseded` | an older revision replaced by a newer one |
| `failed` | the operation errored |
| `pending-install` / `pending-upgrade` / `pending-rollback` | operation in progress (or stuck) |
| `uninstalled` / `uninstalling` | release removed / removing |

### Where the state actually lives
```bash
kubectl get secret -n helm-learn -l owner=helm,name=demo --show-labels
# one secret per revision, type helm.sh/release.v1
# labels: owner=helm, name=demo, status=deployed, version=3
kubectl get secret -n helm-learn \
  -l owner=helm,status=deployed,name=demo \
  -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.labels.version}'    # 3
```

### Namespace scope
`helm list`/`status`/`history` only look at **one namespace** (default or `-n`). Across the cluster:
```bash
helm list -A            # all namespaces
helm list -aA           # all namespaces + all statuses (failed, superseded...)
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Namespace-scoped**: forget `-n` → release "missing." Use `-A` to find it.
- **Revision only increases** — rollback to rev 1 produces rev 4, not rev 1 again.
- **`helm list` hides non-deployed** by default; add `-a/--all` to see `failed`/`superseded`/`pending`.
- **`superseded` is normal** for old revisions — not an error.
- The `version` and `status` **labels on the release Secret** are the source of truth a grader may check directly.
- A stuck `pending-*` status usually means a prior operation was interrupted; `helm rollback` or `--force` may be needed.

### Quick reference
```bash
helm list -n helm-learn                       # REVISION 3, STATUS deployed
helm status demo -n helm-learn
helm history demo -n helm-learn
kubectl get secret -n helm-learn \
  -l owner=helm,status=deployed,name=demo \
  -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.labels.version}'   # 3
```

questions.title: Helm: render a chart without installing (template)
questions.teach:
`helm template <name> <chart>` renders a chart's manifests to stdout **without touching the cluster** — the way to preview or pipe YAML into `kubectl`. `--set`/`-f` apply during render just like on install, so you can verify an override before shipping it.

**Gotcha:** `helm template` does NOT create a release or run server-side — nothing appears in `helm list`; it is purely local rendering.
questions.prompt:
Without creating a release, render your `webapp` chart with `replicaCount=7` and write the output to `/tmp/rendered.yaml` on the host.

Target: file `/tmp/rendered.yaml` exists and contains a Deployment manifest whose rendered `replicas: 7` (and no new release appears in `helm-learn`).

verification.description: /tmp/rendered.yaml contains a rendered Deployment with replicas: 7 (no install performed)

questions.eli5:
Sometimes you want to *see what the furniture would look like assembled* without actually putting it in the room. Like a "print preview" — it shows you every page, but nothing goes to the printer.

`helm template` is Helm's print preview. It takes the chart, fills in all the values, and prints the finished Kubernetes YAML **to your screen**, without touching the cluster. No release is created, nothing is installed. It's perfect for checking "did my override actually land?" before you commit.

```
helm template demo /tmp/webapp --set replicaCount=7 > /tmp/rendered.yaml
```

Your `--set` and `-f` overrides apply during the preview exactly as they would on a real install — so if you render with `replicaCount=7`, the printed Deployment shows `replicas: 7`. You saved it to a file, so you can read it, or even pipe it straight into `kubectl apply -f`.

**Watch out:**

- **`helm template` does NOT create a release.** Nothing shows up in `helm list`, nothing is deployed — it's pure local rendering. Don't expect the cluster to change.
- Because it's local, it mostly **skips the API server** — some server-side checks and lookups (`--validate`, cluster `lookup` functions) don't run unless you ask.
- The **first argument is still a release name** (`demo`) used only to fill in name templates during rendering — it doesn't register anything.
- Redirect to a file with `>` if you want to keep or apply the output; otherwise it just scrolls past on screen.
- Overrides (`--set`/`-f`) behave the same as on install, so previewing is an accurate dry run of what you'd ship.
questions.deepDive:
## Helm: render a chart without installing (`template`) — full rundown

### Mental model
`helm template` renders a chart's templates into final Kubernetes YAML **locally** and prints to stdout — no release, no cluster writes. It's the way to preview output, verify an override, or pipe manifests into `kubectl apply -f -`. Overrides (`--set`, `-f`) apply during rendering exactly as they would on `install`/`upgrade`.

### The command
```bash
helm template demo /tmp/webapp --set replicaCount=7 > /tmp/rendered.yaml
#             ^release-name ^chart   ^override        ^capture to file
grep -n 'replicas: 7' /tmp/rendered.yaml
```
The first arg is a **release name** used only to fill `fullname`/name templates — it registers nothing.

### `helm template` vs `helm install --dry-run`
| | `helm template` | `helm install --dry-run` |
|---|---|---|
| Talks to API server | No (client-side) | Yes (needs a cluster) |
| Creates a release | No | No |
| Runs server validation | Only with `--validate` | Yes |
| `lookup` template function | Returns empty (no cluster) | Works against cluster |
| Use when | offline preview / GitOps render | validate against real cluster |

### Useful flags
| Flag | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `--set k=v`, `-f file` | apply value overrides during render |
| `-s, --show-only templates/deployment.yaml` | render just one template |
| `--namespace ns` | set the namespace in rendered metadata |
| `--validate` | validate against the live cluster's API |
| `--include-crds` | include CRDs from `crds/` in output |
| `--output-dir DIR` | write each manifest to its own file |

### Typical uses
```bash
# preview a single resource:
helm template demo /tmp/webapp -s templates/deployment.yaml

# render and apply in one shot (no Helm release created):
helm template demo /tmp/webapp --set replicaCount=7 | kubectl apply -f -

# GitOps: commit rendered manifests
helm template demo /tmp/webapp -f prod-values.yaml --output-dir ./out
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **No release is created** — nothing in `helm list`, cluster unchanged. This is the key distinction the exam tests.
- **Client-side by default** — `lookup` returns empty and server validation is skipped unless `--validate`.
- **Redirect to keep output**: `> file.yaml` or pipe to `kubectl`; otherwise it only prints.
- The release-name arg is **cosmetic** (feeds name templates); it doesn't install or reserve a name.
- `--dry-run` on `install`/`upgrade` is the *cluster-aware* preview; `template` is the *offline* one — pick based on whether you need server checks.

### Quick reference
```bash
helm template demo /tmp/webapp --set replicaCount=7 > /tmp/rendered.yaml
grep 'replicas: 7' /tmp/rendered.yaml
helm template demo /tmp/webapp -s templates/deployment.yaml   # one template
helm template demo /tmp/webapp | kubectl apply -f -           # render + apply
```
